* * * [T]he shift from ICE to USCIS amounted to DHS 
leadership, presumably in consultation with the White House, 
selecting the agency component more likely to share the views of the 
President and agency leadership and therefore more amenable to 
oversight in its administration of the program. As the benefits- 
granting component of DHS, USCIS is more likely than ICE to be 
institutionally predisposed to viewing unmigrants as claimants with 
potential entitlements; ICE is more likely to see them as lawbreakers.

Legislative Rules Versus Interpretive Rules
Just as an agency may justify bypassing APA section 553’s notice-and- 
comment procedures by claiming that its rule is a policy statement, so it 
may justify bypassing those procedures by claiming that its rule is an 
interpretive rule. But what is an interpretive rule?
In American Mining Congress v. Mine Safety and Health Admin,, 995 
F.2d 1106 (D.C. Cir. 1993), the D.C. Circuit admitted that the distinction 
between legislative rules and interpretive rules was “enshrouded in 
considerable smog” and sought to clear some of it. The court noted that its 
prior decisions on the distinction had asked “whether the disputed rule has 
‘the force of law,’ ” in which case it had to be legislative. But as the opinion 
made clear, “force of law” was not the same as “binding effect,” for binding 
effect was key to the distinction between legislative rules and policy 
statements hut not to the distinction between legislative rules and 
interpretive rules: interpretive rules could have a binding effect. Id. at 
1111; accord Syncorint'l Corp. v. Shalala, 127 F.3d 90, 96 (D.C. Cir. 1999). 
In trying to explain what “force of law” meant, the court said:
* * * We have said that a rule has such force [i.e., the force of 
law] only if Congress has delegated legislative power to the agency 
and if the agency intended to exercise that power in promulgating 
the rule.
On its face, the “intent to exercise” language may seem to lead 
only to more smog, but in fact there are a substantial number of 
instances where such “intent” can be found with some confidence.
